findings.text: The process starts with factory building plan approval (CAF-1) before manufacturing commences, after which the entrepreneur applies for the factory license itself (CAF-2) through the Single Desk Portal.

Site inspection by the Inspector of Factories remains an offline, physical process; virtual/digital inspection is not currently used because physical inspection is considered a more value-added exercise.
The statutory disposal timeline for a factory license application is 7 working days, applied uniformly across hazardous, non-hazardous and general category industries.

No deemed-approval provision is actively invoked; if an application is not disposed of within the 7 working-day window, the concerned Inspector must submit an explanation to the Commissioner of Industries instead. The expert said no deemed-approval situation has arisen so far.

The license is valid for one year, with the renewal fee paid online annually before 31 December; any amendment to the activity (e.g. an additional manufacturing line or increased horsepower) instead requires a Revision License (RVL) with revised plan approval.
The license fee is slab-based, linked to the installed horsepower and the number of workers employed, and is paid online.
About 50-60% of the plan information required for the factory license (CAF-2) auto-populates from the earlier building-plan-approval stage (CAF-1); only the remainder must be submitted afresh.

The Stability Certificate requirement is a frequent point of deficiency: some applicants wrongly assume it is not needed for new buildings and omit it, triggering a deficiency/query (NCS) on the application.

The official recommends improving applicant guidance on mandatory documents (including the Stability Certificate) and clarifying what carries forward from CAF-1 versus what must be freshly submitted for CAF-2, to cut deficiency queries and delays.

Factories, Pollution Control and Labour departments each run separate inspections/certifications on the same establishment; the official considers merging these into one joint inspection or license not feasible since each checks a distinct technical aspect (worker safety, emissions, labour welfare).

Flagged as a best practice: inspection observations and field-visit findings are uploaded to the public domain through the Central Inspection System (CIS) portal, making inspection reports publicly accessible.
The AP Single Window Portal is not truly "single": departments such as electrical sit outside it, so applicants still have to approach them separately.
The portal's 20 MB upload limit is too small for a full drawing set (4-5 drawings plus structural designs); some industries need 50-100 MB and repeatedly have to request an increase.

Applicants, especially small industries without in-house technical knowledge, rely on consultants end-to-end for form filling, submission, query responses and liaisoning; AutoCAD drawings are described as effectively essential.

The building stability study must be obtained at the applicant's own cost from a government-empanelled structural/civil engineer; the fee varies by engineer and industry size, and preparing it takes considerable time.
Category-wise technical specifications and mandatory requirements are not clearly communicated to all applicants.

Participants described there being no true "renewal": the license carries forward January-December once the fee is paid by 30 December, with only an acknowledgement issued rather than a fresh license or certificate.
The portal shows only "pending" or "pending upload" status with no published approval timeline; applicants only learn of approval when the certificate is printed at the very end of the process.
Participants' top-priority ask: introduce real-time, stage-wise application tracking with timelines, modeled on the AP incentive portal.
Raise the portal's 20 MB upload cap to 50-100 MB, and publish an FAQ/guidance document on the portal listing mandatory documents, technical specifications and safety guidelines by industry category.
Participants asked for improved service quality and investment in skill development/skill mapping, explicitly preferring this over any fee reduction.
No unrecorded or informal costs were reported; participants said every cost in the process can be recorded in the books.

Secondary research confirms the 7-working-day statutory timeline with a precise legal citation: Rule 3 of the AP Factories Rules, 1950, as amended by G.O.Ms.No.7/2022 (2 March 2022), which cut the window from 30 days to 7 days and moved filing online via the Single Desk Portal.

Secondary research independently confirms the risk/license threshold: AP's amendment to Section 2(m)/85(1) of the Factories Act sets it at more than 20 workers for factories with power (matching the ED) and 40 workers for factories without power.

Secondary research nuances the ED's "no deemed approval invoked": AP has a state-wide statutory deemed-approval framework for industrial clearances generally (AP Industrial Single Window Clearance Act, 2002), and green/white category industries get deemed approval to commence within 3 years of a self-declared undertaking under the Industrial Policy 2020-23 — so the mechanism exists in law but is rarely invoked for factory licenses specifically, rather than being wholly absent.

gaps.text: Exact INR fee amounts/slab figures for the factory license are not stated anywhere in ED, FGD, or secondary research — only that it is 'slab-based' and linked to horsepower and number of workers. Secondary research notes current fee-schedule figures could not be verified online (only a clearly outdated 1994 reference was found).

The ED transcript states the deadline for submitting a revised plan after a minor deviation is found as 'a stipulated period (e.g., 15 days/1 week)' — two different units given without a single precise figure.

ED frames the service as having an annual 'renewal' with a renewal fee, implying a renewed license. FGD participants instead describe 'no renewal system': the license simply 'carries forward' once the fee is paid by 30 December, and 'only an acknowledgement is issued, not a fresh licence or certificate.' Both describe the same annual fee-payment mechanism but characterize its legal/documentary output differently.
Neither ED nor FGD states how many in-person/office visits an applicant typically needs versus fully online steps; this remains unclear even after cross-checking against the secondary-research field.

The ED's generic 'statutory timeline' of 7 working days is resolved with a precise legal citation by secondary research: Rule 3 of the AP Factories Rules 1950, as amended by G.O.Ms.No.7/2022 (2 Mar 2022), which cut the window from 30 days to 7 days.

The ED's '>20 workers / <10 for specified hazardous categories' risk threshold is independently confirmed by secondary research citing AP's amendment to Sec 2(m)/85(1) of the Factories Act, which also adds the previously-unstated detail that the threshold is 40 workers for factories without power.

Secondary research identified two further 2025 Factories Rules amendments (G.O.Ms.No.19 and G.O.Ms.No.22) and a draft Safety Audit Rules 2025, but their actual content could not be confirmed online, so what (if anything) they change for factory licensing remains unknown.

AP publishes inspection observations and field-visit findings to the public domain via the Central Inspection System (CIS) portal, per the ED's own account — a transparency practice worth other states replicating. Note FGD participants' complaint is about a different kind of transparency (no real-time application-status tracking), so this CIS-level disclosure does not appear to be what applicants experience day to day.
